brief.head: Words nobody opposes
brief.text: Nobody can be seen to favour money laun­der­ing or ter­ror­ist fi­nanc­ing, Ajay Shah said. Under those words India built a sur­veil­lance sys­tem that drags house­holds through end­less KYC. {071-C19}

brief.head: Rule-maker, cop, judge
brief.text: Indian reg­u­la­tors write the rules, en­force them and rule on vi­o­la­tions, Ajay Shah said; India is the only coun­try where reg­u­la­tors also judge. The re­sult is a cli­mate of fear. {071-C15}

brief.head: Finance as the brain
brief.text: Finance is the brain of the econ­omy, Ajay Shah said, so the best minds be­long there; work­ing in a fi­nan­cial firm in­stead of doing par­ti­cle physics is no mis­al­lo­ca­tion. {071-C16}

brief.head: Why Marx feels natural
brief.text: Amit Varma ar­gued that Marx’s ideas will al­ways res­onate more than Hayek’s, be­cause they flat­ter in­stincts for top-down plan­ning, zero-sum think­ing and a strong­man for the tribe. {071-C05}

brief.head: Not Pitroda’s doing

lead.kicker: Ajay Shah and Amit Varma on India’s money since 1947
lead.head: The planners never left the bank

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 71

body: For Ajay Shah, the jour­ney of Indian fi­nance since 1947 comes down to one di­ag­no­sis: “an in­tel­lec­tual fail­ure of the Indian elite to build the knowl­edge and com­mu­nity around words like mar­ket fail­ure, cen­tral plan­ning, rule of law, state ca­pa­bil­ity”. {071-C06}
Shah told the story as a chap­ter for a Cambridge his­tory of mod­ern South Asia. Amit Varma called it “the de­fin­i­tive work on the sub­ject”.

It starts with cen­tral plan­ning. If the gov­ern­ment de­cides prod­ucts and pro­cesses, Shah said, that is cen­tral plan­ning, and after in­de­pen­dence bank­ing be­came one ex­tended plan­ning sys­tem. Delhi li­censed the steel mill; Bombay’s bu­reau­cracy sup­plied the credit.
“The RBI be­came the cen­tral plan­ning shop of the fi­nan­cial sec­tor,” he said.

Officials spoke un­em­bar­rassed of re­source mo­bil­i­sa­tion: tak­ing households’ money and giv­ing it to “our cho­sen ones”. A one-size-fits-all bu­reau­cracy, Shah ar­gued, serves only the top in­come decile. “You are harm­ing the in­ter­ests of ninety per­cent of India,” he said. {071-C02}
## Stars and lag­gards

Banking stayed a dis­ap­point­ment. After decades of fail­ing to learn bank reg­u­la­tion and res­o­lu­tion, Shah would rather India did not bet on a large bank­ing sys­tem, and grew fi­nance through bond mar­kets, NBFCs and for­eign banks in­stead.
“If we are a third world coun­try and we don’t know how to run air traf­fic con­trol, then maybe you should not have so much air travel,” he said. {071-C04}

The eq­uity mar­ket was the star pupil. SEBI, NSE and the de­pos­i­tory NSDL, built from the late 1980s to the mid-1990s, made what Shah called one of the great suc­cess sto­ries of the Indian re­forms.

Mutual funds came out rea­son­ably well. Insurance was medi­ocre, pen­sions saw major re­ver­sals, and cap­i­tal con­trols sur­vived the re­forms: FEMA, which re­placed FERA in 1999, be­gins by ban­ning all trans­ac­tions.
## Who looks after a re­form?

Why did the good re­forms fade? Shah’s an­swer is knowl­edge and com­mu­nity. The eq­uity re­forms were car­ried by a team across the fi­nance min­istry, SEBI, NSE and aca­demic in­sti­tu­tions, who ar­gued in blogs, op-eds and sem­i­nars.
When that team was bro­ken up, he said, the com­mu­nity was thrown away and India went back to “a nor­mal bum­bling world of pol­i­cy­mak­ing”. {071-C17}
Pension re­form with­ered out of inat­ten­tion. Inflation tar­get­ing, he warned, could be next, with many on the left back to snip­ing at it.
The hosts parted ways over bailouts. Varma, who wants the state never to bail any­one out, told Shah: “To me, you are a lefty.”
## Three phases
Shah sees three phases: ex­plicit so­cial­ism from 1947 to 1991; then, until per­haps 2016, real knowl­edge-building mixed with ex­u­ber­ant la­bels; and now a mud­dle.

Throughout, India has prac­tised iso­mor­phic mimicry, build­ing in­sti­tu­tions that look right from out­side. “You can show a gullible for­eign vis­i­tor that oh we have a bond mar­ket,” he said. Officials still ef­fec­tively set every in­ter­est rate. {071-C18}

His own views have moved. The young Shah cheered press re­leases; the older one reads the laws, and finds the devil in im­ple­men­ta­tion, the land of pub­lic choice, state ca­pa­bil­ity and rule of law.
The task now, he said, is a 25-year jour­ney of build­ing knowl­edge and build­ing com­mu­nity.
Varma ended by rec­om­mend­ing the paper, and its au­thor, a man once “greatly re­spected by all as an econ­o­mist, till he turned a YouTuber and started doing con­tent”.

second.label: Banks and computers
second.head: Disk by decree
second.deck: How an RBI committee wrote the IT strategy of every bank in India

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the Rangarajan Committee’s hardware

body: When com­put­ers ar­rived in the early 1990s, the Reserve Bank of India de­cided that banks needed com­put­er­i­sa­tion. The Rangarajan Committee then wrote down ex­actly what every bank had to do, Ajay Shah said. {071-S01}

It named the CPU and the disk con­troller: an SMD con­troller, for Uniplus Unix ma­chines with Motorola 68K pro­ces­sors. “You could lit­er­ally take the RBI re­port and it be­came the IT strat­egy of every bank,” Shah said.

Nobody was em­bar­rassed, be­cause pre­scrib­ing tech­nol­ogy was seen as RBI’s job. For Shah, of­fi­cials pick­ing win­ners is “a com­plete red line”. Amit Varma saw the same mind­set in a sin­gle state-backed pay­ment sys­tem today. {#dpi}

quote.text: They chose the name of the CPU. They chose the name of the disc con­troller which will be in­side every bank.

third.head: Credit comes to the cinema

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the loan at the movies

body: Ajay Shah was in the au­di­ence at an Indian Express event with KV Kamath and Mukesh Ambani on stage. Shekhar Gupta asked Ambani what he had seen change over the re­form years.
In the bad old days, Ambani said, his driver had to come to him for a loan. {071-S13} Recently, when he went to watch a movie at Metro, a teenager plucked his sleeve and asked if he wanted one.

Household credit, Shah said, is one of the real suc­cesses of Indian fi­nance. Credit bu­reaus changed borrowers’ in­cen­tives by record­ing de­faults, and pri­vate NBFCs took loans to house­holds across the coun­try.

Amit Varma passed on a worry, from Harsh Vardhan among oth­ers, that con­sumer credit had ex­ploded un­sus­tain­ably. Shah called the re­cent debt-fuelled spell “a small glitch in a larger jour­ney”. {#glitch}

box.title: The paper behind the episode
box.text: Ajay Shah’s Table 2, a one-page chronol­ogy of mile­stones across every sec­tor, is the part ev­ery­body loves, he says. The paper began as a chap­ter for *The Cambridge Economic History of Modern South Asia*, and Amit Varma calls it “al­most a mag­is­te­rial ac­count”. {071-R01}

sections.label: Banking
sections.head: One little super bank
sections.caption: banking as central planning
body: Indian bank­ing was na­tion­alised in stages, from SBI to the sweeps of 1969 and 1980. Ajay Shah traced the idea to the 1848 *Communist Manifesto*, which called for credit cen­tralised in a state mo­nop­oly bank. “Some aca­demic scrib­bler in the years gone by shapes the mad­man in frenzy,” he said. {071-J02}
Each gap in the planned sys­tem got a new pub­lic sec­tor mo­nop­oly: IDBI, ICICI, HDFC. Shah would have let a hun­dred busi­ness mod­els com­pete and ninety-five go bust.

By the early 1990s, he said, RBI had re­alised that bank­ing reg­u­la­tion ex­isted and that it knew noth­ing about it. A Rs 5,500 crore hole found in­side Indian Bank in 1995 started the learn­ing. {071-S02}
## Two things to get right

Regulation, Shah said, comes down to two things. Value loans hon­estly: if a loan of 100 would fetch 80 at auc­tion today, book the 20 loss now. And hold enough eq­uity. Indian banks run about five of eq­uity against 95 of de­posits, too thin for India’s volatile econ­omy, and a ratio that made bribery pay at fam­ily-run banks, most of which failed. {071-C03}

Honest val­u­a­tion drags bad news into the open, which a plan­ner re­sists. “In a cen­tral plan­ning sys­tem, RBI is mother,” Shah said. “Mother can­not allow bad news to be told to the pub­lic.” {071-J03}
~ Since 1992, about five per cent of one year’s GDP has gone as gov­ern­ment money to the pub­lic sec­tor banks: credit un­der­priced, Shah said, and paid for by the tax­payer. {#gdp5}

quote.text: It is too easy to give out loans of hun­dred and take bribes of ten.

sections.label: Equity markets
sections.head: Trucks full of paper
sections.caption: the stock market reforms
body: The Bombay Stock Exchange, run by a club of mostly Gujarati and Marwari bro­kers, did lit­tle after in­de­pen­dence. Yet India had had the first stock mar­ket of Asia, Ajay Shah said, in 1874. {#bse1874}

The club could not set­tle trades on a pre­dictable clock, and some mem­bers were hand in glove with mar­ket ma­nip­u­la­tors. Shah is still trou­bled that its 300 to 400 bro­kers never struck a deal among them­selves to mod­ernise their own ex­change. {071-C07}
So the state stepped in, with SEBI from 1988, NSE from 1992 and the de­pos­i­tory NSDL from 1995.
## Software needed shares

The new mar­ket mat­tered most to new in­dus­tries. Banks would not lend to early soft­ware firms, which had no fac­tory to pledge. Shah draws a di­rect line from the Infosys IPO of 1994 to NSE and SEBI. {071-S04}

The old sys­tem had choked on small sums. In August and September 1993, for­eign money began ar­riv­ing at about $100 mil­lion a month, and the streets of Bombay filled with “truck­loads of share cer­tifi­cates”. {071-S05}

~ Shah ranks the eq­uity mar­ket along­side the tele­com re­forms and Major General Khanduri’s National Highways Authority as he­roes of the re­form era. That team, he said, has since been bro­ken up.

quote.text: Why were these peo­ple not able to come to­gether and find a Coasian bar­gain and do that ne­go­ti­a­tion be­tween them­selves

sections.label: Currency controls
sections.head: Money that may not leave
sections.caption: capital controls
body: In the first glob­al­i­sa­tion there were no cap­i­tal con­trols, Ajay Shah said, and bond is­sues in London built India’s rail­ways. Then the British im­posed cur­rency re­stric­tions in 1939, and Indira Gandhi amended the 1947 for­eign ex­change law in 1973 to add crim­i­nal con­se­quences. {#fera1973}
Shah treats the free­dom to move wealth as a human right: leav­ing a coun­try, as a Jewish refugee left Germany, means lit­tle if your wealth stays trapped.

The eco­nom­ics is just as plain. Capital is the big­gest cost in a ton of steel, big­ger than iron ore or coal, and spread­ing in­vest­ments world­wide low­ers risk. “The dream of eco­nom­ics is that you, Amit Bhai, should own a flat in Tokyo that you rent to a Japanese guy,” Shah told Amit Varma. {071-C08}
## A law that starts with no

FEMA, the 1999 law that re­placed FERA, be­gins by ban­ning all trans­ac­tions. In 1993, when India an­nounced cur­rent ac­count con­vert­ibil­ity, the young Shah cheered; years later he read the laws and found it did not exist. {071-S09}
In prac­tice, those who can pay lawyers and ac­coun­tants get open­ness, and ev­ery­body else is shut out. Varma called it a clas­sic case of the lack of free­dom hurt­ing the poor first. {071-C09}
~ Varma wanted a Foreign Exchange Freedom Act in­stead. Of “reg­u­la­tion” and “man­age­ment”, Shah said: “I don’t know which word is more of­fen­sive.” {071-J07}

quote.text: This is a clas­sic il­lus­tra­tion of how the lack of free­dom al­ways hurts the poor first.

sections.label: Bankruptcy
sections.head: Ice cubes melt, so hurry
sections.caption: bankruptcy and the melting ice cube
body: Firms must be able to fail, Ajay Shah said, or there is no real com­pe­ti­tion. The ques­tion is whether they fail badly, in a power play where “the per­son with the most gun­das grabs as­sets”, or by a pre­dictable script that ev­ery­one signs up to in ad­vance. {071-C10}

He of­fered a magic pair of ideas. When a firm fails, the loss has al­ready hap­pened: if 100 of cap­i­tal is now worth 40, the only ques­tion is who gets the 40. And a firm in dis­tress melts, as ven­dors go un­paid, ma­chines go un­main­tained and staff walk away. {071-C11}
## Never re­pos­sessed

India had lit­tle of this. In the late 1990s Deepak Parekh, head of HDFC, told Shah that it had never re­pos­sessed a house. Lenders got the power to seize col­lat­eral only with SARFAESI in 2002. {071-S11}

The bank­ruptcy code began when KP Krishnan took a sec­tion of the 2015 bud­get speech to Arun Jaitley and sug­gested blow­ing it up into a full code. TK Viswanathan led the com­mit­tee; Shah and Susan were mem­bers, and Susan led the draft­ing. {071-S12}
The re­sult has been luke­warm, Shah said: RBI steers banks away from the code, im­ple­men­ta­tion has fal­tered at IBBI and NCLT, and the re­form com­mu­nity dis­persed.
~ Shah quoted Hemingway: asked how he went bank­rupt, a char­ac­ter an­swers, “slowly at first and then sud­denly”. {071-J20}

quote.text: So you want to rec­og­nize that speed is of essence be­cause a firm going into death is a melt­ing ice cube.

sections.label: Systemic risk
sections.head: Crises, made in India
sections.caption: crises made at home
body: Ajay Shah used to think of sys­temic crises as global shocks: Asia in 1997, LTCM, 2008. Now he says “the Indian fi­nan­cial sys­tem is en­tirely ca­pa­ble of gen­er­at­ing a sys­temic cri­sis all on its own”. {071-C13}

Three fail­ures in­ter­act, he said: mon­e­tary pol­icy that is not in­fla­tion tar­get­ing, weak pru­den­tial reg­u­la­tion, and no way to shut failed firms. The cen­tral bank ends up “pour­ing LSD in the punch when the party gets going”. {071-J11}
His paper finds six sys­temic crises from 1992 to 2018, among them Andhra Pradesh’s 2010 ban on mi­cro­fi­nance. {#sixcrises}
Shah even found Indian money in Oscar Wilde’s *The Importance of Being Earnest*, from 1895: “The chap­ter on the fall of the rupee you may omit.” {071-J19}
## To bail or not

At any mo­ment, Shah said, reg­u­la­tors are good at fight­ing the last war. Clever peo­ple op­ti­mise around every rule, so some crises are a price worth pay­ing for the growth fi­nance brings. {071-C12}
Amit Varma dis­agreed. Bailouts pri­va­tise prof­its and so­cialise losses, he said, and every one is a tax on the poor; the state should never bail any­one out.
Shah partly con­ceded. In many, many things, he said, the cor­rect an­swer is to let go and take moral haz­ard se­ri­ously.
~ Varma had just called him a lefty. Shah’s reply: “You are a man after my own heart.”

quote.text: If there is sys­temic risk, let the frick­ing sys­tem fail so the next time it doesn’t hap­pen.

And that en­tire team was dis­rupted and we’ve thrown away that com­mu­nity, we’ve thrown away that team, and we’re re­ally back to a nor­mal bum­bling world of pol­i­cy­mak­ing and then many things start going wrong.

p3.title: Tales of the reform years
p3.deck: A keystroke, a payphone, a green line and a bankruptcy nobody noticed

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah remembers the day the depository opened
stories.head: Five minutes, years in the making
body: In August and September 1993, the first surge of for­eign in­vest­ment reached India at about $100 mil­lion a month. The Bombay Stock Exchange choked on it, and trucks car­ried paper share cer­tifi­cates through the streets. {#hundredmillion}

Foreign in­vestors could not work with that. Part of the an­swer was NSDL, a stock de­pos­i­tory, and it needed an en­abling law: the Depositories Act, “a beau­ti­ful law”, Ajay Shah said, drafted by PJ Nayak and M Sahu.
But it had to pass Parliament, and the gov­ern­ment of the day did not have a ma­jor­ity.

Help came from an un­likely quar­ter. The British Chancellor of the Exchequer met Manmohan Singh and raised the law as a real choke point. Singh, in turn, pressed the Congress po­lit­i­cal es­tab­lish­ment to get it through by hook or by crook. “I don’t know what means were ap­plied,” Shah said, “but they got that law through.”

On 6 November 1996, Shah was in the au­di­to­rium at Nehru Centre for the in­au­gu­ra­tion. On stage, as he re­mem­bers it, were Bimal Jalan, the RBI gov­er­nor; DR Mehta, the SEBI chair­man; CB Bhave, the depository’s MD; and P Chidambaram.
Somebody pressed one car­riage re­turn to pre­tend that a first trans­ac­tion had taken place. Chidambaram hugged Bhave. “So the en­tire cer­e­mony was five min­utes,” Shah said. {071-S06}
~ He counts it among the hap­pi­est days of his life. The whole tale, Amit Varma said, is told at greater length in their ten-and-a-half-hour episode of *The Seen and the Unseen*.
stories.why: Big in­sti­tu­tional change looks tiny on the day it ar­rives. Behind one key­stroke lay years of draft­ing, per­sua­sion and po­lit­i­cal deal-making by a small group of peo­ple: the knowl­edge and com­mu­nity Shah calls the real en­gine of re­form. {071-C17}
stories.postscript: Told it was one of Shah’s hap­pi­est days, Amit Varma replied: “It’s so easy to make you happy.” {071-J04}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the five-minute launch of NSDL

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on what telecom shows about banking
stories.head: One payphone, every village
body: Telecom was once as tidy as Indian bank­ing, Ajay Shah said: a gov­ern­ment mo­nop­oly of the Department of Telecommunications, MTNL, BSNL and VSNL, de­fended in the name of na­tional se­cu­rity. The rich got phones after a ten-year wait or a bribe. Most of India got none.
The of­fi­cial dream was a vil­lage tele­phone scheme: one pay­phone in every vil­lage, where you threw in a coin, made one call and could not call long dis­tance. {071-S03}

Then Sudhindra Kulkarni and Arun Shourie, work­ing in the Vajpayee gov­ern­ment, opened the sec­tor to pri­vate and for­eign play­ers. Mobile calls that once cost six­teen ru­pees a minute be­came a “janta prod­uct”, and India now has about 1.1 bil­lion tele­phones for 1.4 bil­lion peo­ple. {#telephones}
~ Banking, Shah said, missed out on all that en­ergy. Run as a bu­reau­cracy, it stayed ex­actly as dead as tele­com had been.
stories.why: A bu­reau­cratic mo­nop­oly serves only the elite, while com­pe­ti­tion reaches the whole coun­try. Telecom, for Shah, is the coun­ter­fac­tual for na­tion­alised bank­ing, whose one-size-fits-all de­sign served only the top decile. {071-C02}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the village payphone

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how Britain locked in capital freedom
stories.head: Thatcher rubs out the green line
body: When Margaret Thatcher’s Britain opened its cur­rent and cap­i­tal ac­counts, Ajay Shah said, some peo­ple pro­posed a com­pro­mise: free ev­ery­thing, but make peo­ple sub­mit some data.

You would stand in a queue, sub­mit a form and get au­to­matic ac­cess to a green line. The re­form­ers re­fused. Keep the re­port­ing, they ar­gued, and a fu­ture gov­ern­ment could eas­ily shut the gate again. “The point is to de­stroy the green line,” Shah said.
So in the early 1980s Britain re­moved the re­port­ing re­quire­ments too, “so that in the fu­ture no lefty will be able to bring back the cap­i­tal con­trols”. {071-S08}
~ India did the op­po­site. It kept its ap­pa­ra­tus of con­trol when FEMA re­placed FERA, and sure enough, in 2015 the crim­i­nal clauses came back. {#criminal2015}
stories.why: Reforms must be built to be hard to re­verse. Leave the forms and the queue in place, Shah’s story sug­gests, and a later gov­ern­ment will find it easy to switch the con­trols back on.
stories.postscript: Amit Varma’s favourite story: at her first cab­i­net meet­ing, Thatcher threw down Hayek’s *The Constitution of Liberty* and said, “This is what we be­lieve in.” {071-J22}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Thatcher and the green line

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how Europe’s telecom firms failed quietly
stories.head: Bust, without a dropped call
body: European tele­com firms were over-optimistic about the 2G auc­tions, Ajay Shah said, and bid ridicu­lous sums of money for spec­trum li­cences. The rev­enue never came, and the firms went bank­rupt.
Their cus­tomers no­ticed noth­ing. “Our phones con­tin­ued to work, our phone num­bers stayed,” Shah said. “We never got a missed call. We never got a dropped call.” {071-S10}
Somewhere up in the fi­nan­cial su­per­struc­ture, the old share­hold­ers and bond­hold­ers took the losses, and new share­hold­ers picked up the firms as going con­cerns.
~ In India, Shah said, the years go by and the firm is de­stroyed be­fore any­thing hap­pens. Caught early, he ar­gued, per­haps 80 or 90 per cent of firms would be worth sav­ing. {#ninety}

quote.text: That’s the dream of bank­ruptcy, that some firms are wor­thy of res­cu­ing.

glossary.def: Institutions that look right from out­side but lack the sub­stance.
A pri­vate deal among par­ties to fix a shared prob­lem.
A thug; in bad bank­rupt­cies, who­ever has most grabs as­sets.
Non-performing asset: a bank loan that has gone bad.
A prod­uct for ev­ery­one, as mo­bile phones be­came.
Set rules, and clever peo­ple will op­ti­mise around them.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 71. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Margaret Thatcher (derivative work by Begoon, Copyrighted free use); Karl Marx (John Jabez Edwin Mayall, public domain); Ernest Hemingway (Lloyd Arnold, public domain); Friedrich Hayek (Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0); R. K. Narayan (R. K. Balaraman (photographer), public domain). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon and Open Library.

shelf.title: The Journey of Indian Finance
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s eco­nomic his­tory of Indian fi­nance from 1947 to today, which Amit calls close to mag­is­te­rial and the de­fin­i­tive work on the sub­ject.

shelf.title: The Cambridge Economic History of Modern South Asia
shelf.creator: Edited by Latika Chaudhary, Tirthankar Roy and Anand Swamy
shelf.why: He has seen the table of con­tents and calls it ‘drool’.

shelf.title: Capital Ideas
shelf.creator: Peter Bernstein
shelf.why: A lovely, if slightly dated, story of how the ideas of mod­ern fi­nance emerged once mod­els and com­put­ers came in; Ajay calls it ‘just great fun’.

shelf.title: The Financial Expert
shelf.creator: RK Narayan
shelf.why: Ajay read it as a child, and it was where he first began think­ing about a run on a bank.

shelf.title: Ajay Shah Brings the Dreams of the 20th Century (Ep 402, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A ten-and-a-half-hour con­ver­sa­tion with Ajay about his life and ideas, in­clud­ing the in­side story of how India built a good eq­uity mar­ket through SEBI, NSE and NSDL.

shelf.title: The Long Road to Change (Ep 36, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ the­ory of change: pol­icy im­proves through a decades-long pipe­line of data, re­search, rival pro­pos­als, pub­lic de­bate, com­mit­tee re­ports and draft laws, not by whis­per­ing in a joint secretary’s ear.

shelf.title: The Beauty of Finance (Ep 21, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s mas­ter­class on why fi­nance ex­ists and why it mat­ters to the real econ­omy: fi­nance as ‘the brain of the economy’, not a casino for the rich, traced back to me­dieval trad­ing voy­ages.

shelf.title: Inflation Targeting Rocks! (Ep 68, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The full story of in­fla­tion tar­get­ing, which Ajay pushed for from the 1990s and which took more than fif­teen years to be­come law: a les­son in how slowly good pol­icy ar­rives.

shelf.title: Beware of These Five Fallacies! (Ep 45, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: How in­stincts evolved in small hunter-gatherer tribes mis­lead us in large, com­plex so­ci­eties: zero-sum think­ing, top-down think­ing, blind­ness to spon­ta­neous order and the pull of strong lead­ers.

shelf.title: Larry White & the First Principles of Money (Ep 397, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Lawrence White’s mas­ter­class on free bank­ing: banks is­su­ing their own com­pet­ing cur­ren­cies ran for decades in parts of the world with­out chaos.

shelf.title: SVB, Banking and the State of the Economy (Ep 323, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah & Mohit Satyanand
shelf.why: Ajay and Mohit Satyanand on the SVB col­lapse and bank­ing fun­da­men­tals, in­clud­ing the coun­ter­in­tu­itive case that bank fail­ures are part of a healthy sys­tem, and how elec­tronic pay­ments let a bank’s money flee over a week­end.

shelf.title: The Importance of the 1991 Reforms (Ep 237, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Rajagopalan & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Shruti Rajagopalan and Ajay on what 1991 achieved and left un­done (fac­tor mar­kets, agri­cul­ture), and how free­ing parts of the econ­omy set off the dis­cov­ery and trade be­hind India’s growth spurt.

shelf.title: The Bankable Wisdom of Harsh Vardhan (Ep 352, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Harsh Vardhan, whom Ajay calls a deep thinker on banks, ar­gues that bank­ing, mag­i­cal and fun­da­men­tally frag­ile, is es­sen­tial to a suc­cess­ful cap­i­tal­ism.

shelf.title: Why Freedom Matters (Ep 10, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Despite the title, an eco­nomic his­tory of India told through the lens of free­dom: the boom after 1869, Nehru’s Fabian so­cial­ism, the lost years from the 1962 war to the Emergency, and the open­ing-up that lifted mil­lions out of poverty.

shelf.title: India’s Pensions Disaster (Ep 65, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A first-principles ac­count of pen­sion re­form: how a small com­mu­nity with a shared phi­los­o­phy built the NPS, and how guar­an­tees and the old mess re­turned once that com­mu­nity dis­persed and its knowl­edge faded.

shelf.title: The 3 Globalizations (Ep 17, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s frame­work of three glob­al­i­sa­tions, from the first era with­out cap­i­tal con­trols, when London bond is­sues built Indian rail­ways, to today’s, where ac­cess to the ad­vanced-economy core de­pends on good be­hav­iour in mil­i­tary and for­eign af­fairs.

shelf.title: Ajay Shah & Bhargavi Zaveri’s article on current account convertibility
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah & Bhargavi Zaveri
shelf.why: Ajay and Bhargavi Zaveri-Shah show that India’s of­fi­cial claim of cur­rent ac­count con­vert­ibil­ity is not true once you read the ac­tual rules and laws, part of Ajay’s case that the Indian state treats cross-border ac­tiv­ity as sus­pect.

shelf.title: Nidhi Aggarwal, Sanchit Arora & Rajeshwari Sengupta’s paper on de facto capital account openness
shelf.creator: Nidhi Aggarwal, Sanchit Arora & Rajeshwari Sengupta
shelf.why: Shows India’s de facto open­ness to for­eign cap­i­tal ris­ing over the years until India is more open than China: cap­i­tal con­trols don’t close the econ­omy, they just make the rich pay lawyers and ac­coun­tants.

shelf.title: The Constitution of Liberty
shelf.creator: Friedrich Hayek
shelf.why: Hayek’s case for free­dom, the book Margaret Thatcher used to de­clare her government’s creed.

shelf.title: The Life & Times of KP Krishnan (Ep 355, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: An eight-hour oral his­tory from a re­former in­side the Indian state: how India han­dled the 2008 cri­sis, fought for in­fla­tion tar­get­ing and built the bank­ruptcy code.

shelf.title: Bhargavi Zaveri-Shah Will Not Wear a Blue Tie to Work (Ep 389, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Bhargavi Zaveri-Shah on fi­nan­cial pri­vacy and the in­side story of how an­a­lysts and wonks came to­gether to draft India’s bank­ruptcy code, which Amit calls ab­so­lutely in­spir­ing.

shelf.title: The Hollow Man
shelf.creator: John Dickson Carr
shelf.why: A 1935 crime novel voted the great­est locked-room mur­der mys­tery of all time.

shelf.title: The Sun Also Rises
shelf.creator: Ernest Hemingway
shelf.why: Its ex­change on going bank­rupt, ‘slowly at first and then suddenly’, is the clas­sic de­scrip­tion of how dis­tress plays out.

shelf.title: The Good Lion
shelf.creator: Ernest Hemingway
shelf.why: A Hemingway story Amit loves, about a lion who badly wants a Hindu trader sand­wich.

shelf.title: Public Choice Theory Explains SO MUCH (Ep 33, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Explains that politi­cians and bu­reau­crats re­spond to in­cen­tives like ev­ery­one else, so the state is no benev­o­lent beast and gov­ern­ment fail­ure is far more com­mon than mar­ket fail­ure.

shelf.title: What Really Happened?
shelf.creator: Larry White
shelf.why: Larry White’s essay on how easy money, bad gov­ern­ment in­cen­tives and quasi-government en­ti­ties caused the 2008 cri­sis, usu­ally called a mar­ket fail­ure.

shelf.title: Not What They Had in Mind
shelf.creator: Arnold Kling
shelf.why: Arnold Kling’s book-length case that the 2008 cri­sis was a fail­ure of the state, driven by over­reach rather than free mar­kets.

shelf.title: Unchecked and Unbalanced
shelf.creator: Arnold Kling
shelf.why: More of Kling’s scep­ti­cal anal­y­sis, which backs Amit’s worry that re­ac­tive state in­ter­ven­tion makes the next cri­sis worse.

shelf.title: The Problem With Digital Public Goods (Ep 56, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A cri­tique of ‘dig­i­tal pub­lic infrastructure’ such as Aadhaar and UPI: state-backed mo­nop­o­lies cre­ated by co­er­cive power, with­out checks and bal­ances, that crowd out com­pet­ing pri­vate sys­tems.

shelf.title: Premature Imitation & India’s Flailing State
shelf.creator: Shruti Rajagopalan & Alex Tabarrok
shelf.why: A ‘great paper’ on why India copies the forms of ad­vanced-economy pol­icy from Britain, the US or Sweden too early and ends up with a flail­ing state, build­ing on Lant Pritchett’s idea of iso­mor­phic mimicry.

shelf.title: Elite Imitation in Public Policy (Ep 180, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Rajagopalan & Alex Tabarrok
shelf.why: Shruti Rajagopalan and Alex Tabarrok on why poli­cies that Indian elites copy from abroad fail in India: a long con­ver­sa­tion about their pre­ma­ture-imitation the­sis.

laughs.text: Ajay on why RBI hides bank­ing trou­ble: ‘In a cen­tral plan­ning sys­tem, RBI is mother. Mother can­not allow bad news to be told to the pub­lic.’
After Ajay calls the five-minute NSDL launch, one key­stroke and a hug, one of the hap­pi­est days of his life, Amit replies: ‘It’s so easy to make you happy.’

Amit: ‘Once upon a time you were the young Turk of Finance. Now you’re just a mid­dle aged Indian sit­ting on a lawn.’ Then: ‘Now I’m just a YouTuber.’ ‘Now you’re just a YouTuber, even worse.’ Amit’s clos­ing rec­om­men­da­tion keeps it going, prais­ing a man ‘greatly re­spected by all as an econ­o­mist, till he turned a YouTuber and started doing con­tent. His name is Ajay Shah.’

Oscar Wilde, The Importance of Being Earnest (1895): Miss Prism tells Cecily, ‘you will read your po­lit­i­cal econ­omy in my ab­sence. The chap­ter on the fall of the rupee you may omit. It is some­what too sen­sa­tional. Even these metal­lic prob­lems have their melo­dra­matic side.’ Indian mon­e­tary pol­icy had made it into a Wilde play.
Hemingway, The Sun Also Rises, the line ev­ery­one in bank­ruptcy quotes: asked how he went bank­rupt, the char­ac­ter an­swers, ‘slowly at first and then sud­denly.’
